title: 青玉案·元夕
author: Xin Qiji

translation: The east wind at night bursts open a thousand trees of flowers
And blows down stars like rain
Fine steeds and carved carriages, fragrance fills the road
The moon's jade pot turns its light
All night, fish and dragon lanterns dance
Moth-ornaments, snow-willows, threads of gold in their hair
Laughing, chatting, they pass, leaving a trail of hidden scent
In the crowd I searched for her a thousand times
Where the lantern light was dimmest

annotations.元夕: the Lantern Festival — 15th night of the first lunar month
annotations.花千树: a thousand trees of flowers — the blaze of countless lanterns and fireworks
annotations.星如雨: stars falling like rain — sparks of fireworks
annotations.玉壶: jade pot — a metaphor for the moon
annotations.蛾儿雪柳黄金缕: women's festival ornaments — moth hairpins, willow threads, gold filigree
annotations.阑珊: lán shān — fading, dying down, sparse

appreciation: Xin Qiji spends eleven lines building the loudest, brightest, most crowded night of the year — fireworks, music, perfume, dancing lanterns — then finds the person he was looking for standing alone where the light is dimmest. The twist at the end is so perfect that '蓦然回首，那人却在灯火阑珊处' became the Chinese language's way of saying: what you seek is found when you stop chasing the noise.
